title: Rhythm and Meter
objective: After this level you can hear stressed and unstressed syllables and recognize iambic pentameter.
summary: Meter counts stresses in feet: an iamb rises (to-DAY), a trochee falls (MAT-ter). Five iambs make iambic pentameter, Shakespeare's line; unrhymed, it is blank verse.

cards.headline: Say "today" out loud. You just spoke an iamb.
cards.body: You didn't say TO-day. You said to-DAY: a soft beat, then a strong one. English is full of these ups and downs, and poets have been counting them for centuries. The counting has a name.

cards.headline: A ruler for the ear
cards.body: Meter, from the Greek metron, "measure," is the measured pattern of stresses in a line of verse. Poets count it in feet: small units of stressed and unstressed syllables. An iamb goes da-DUM, like "today." A trochee flips it, DUM-da, like "matter." Greek prefixes then count the feet in a line: tetrameter has four, pentameter five, hexameter six.

cards.headline: Five iambs in a row
cards.body: Line up five iambs and you get iambic pentameter: about ten syllables that rise five times. Shakespeare wrote his plays and sonnets in it. Hear it in Sonnet 73: "that TIME of YEAR thou MAYST in ME be-HOLD." Drop the rhyme and it becomes blank verse, the standard line for Shakespeare and for John Milton. Five soft-loud steps, and you're speaking in Shakespeare's rhythm.

cards.fact: Flip the foot and the beat lands first.
cards.context: Not every poem rises. Edgar Allan Poe's "The Raven" runs on trochees, stress first: DUM-da, DUM-da. William Blake wrote in trochaic meter too. Hold on to Blake: he comes back at the end of this chapter, and you'll hear the difference the moment you read him aloud.

cards.headline: Meter: measured
learned: Meter measures stressed and unstressed syllables
Iambic pentameter: five iambs a line

options.label: A stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one
An unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one
Two stressed syllables side by side
options.rationale: An iamb has one of each.

questions.explanation: An iamb goes da-DUM, unstressed then stressed, as in "today."

questions.prompt: How can you tell a line is in iambic pentameter?

options.label: It rhymes with the line before it
options.rationale: Meter is about stress, not rhyme.

options.label: It has six feet, each stressed then unstressed
options.rationale: That mixes up hexameter and trochees.

options.label: It has five feet, each a soft beat then a strong one
It has exactly five words
options.rationale: Feet are counted in syllables, not words.

questions.explanation: Iambic pentameter is five iambs: about ten syllables that go soft-loud five times.

questions.prompt: In Level 6, Homer's formulas fit set places in his meter. How long was each line of that meter?
questions.explanation: Homer's meter was the dactylic hexameter, and hexameter means six feet to a line.
